title: El Niño is Back, and Ocean Temperatures are Already Near Record Highs, Which Can Spell Disaster for Fish and Corals
author: Dillon Amaya
content:
[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/06/EL18p-Reunion.jpg)](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/06/25/el-
nino-is-back-and-ocean-temperatures-are-already-near-record-highs-which-can-
spell-disaster-for-fish-and-corals/)

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/EL18p-Reunion.jpg)

Bleached coral covered with. algae. Wikimedia Commons. [CC BY-SA 2.0
fr](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/2.0/fr/deed.en)

It’s official: [El Niño is back](https://www.noaa.gov/news-release/el-nino-
forms-expected-to-strengthen-say-noaa-forecasters). By late fall 2026,
forecast models give a 2-in-3 chance of a strong-to-very strong El Niño
affecting the weather, climate and ocean temperatures across the planet.

El Niño is the climate system’s biggest player and one side of the [El Niño-
Southern Oscillation, or ENSO](https://www.climate.gov/news-
features/understanding-climate/el-ni%C3%B1o-and-la-ni%C3%B1a-frequently-asked-
questions). It’s the heads to La Niña’s tails.

During El Niño, a swath of ocean stretching 6,000 miles (about 10,000
kilometers) westward off the coast of Ecuador warms for months on end,
typically by 2 to 4 degrees Fahrenheit (about 1 to 2 degrees Celsius). A few
degrees may not seem like much, but in that part of the world, it’s more than
enough to completely reorganize wind, rainfall and temperature patterns all
over the planet.

I’m a [climate
scientist](https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=e6h9KeIAAAAJ&hl=en) who
studies the oceans. With an [El Niño expected to strengthen through the summer
and
fall](https://cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/products/analysis_monitoring/enso/roni/strengths/),
water temperatures will heat up even more. It’s time to start preparing.

**How does El Niño affect the planet?**

No two El Niño events are exactly alike, though we’ve seen enough of them that
forecasters have a pretty good idea of [what’s likely to
happen](https://www.weather.gov/images/fwd/climate/enso/ElNino.png).

People tend to focus on El Niño’s impact on land, justifiably. The warm water
affects air currents that leave areas wetter or drier than usual. It can ramp
up storms in some areas, like the southern U.S., while [tending to tamp down
Atlantic hurricane
activity](https://tropical.colostate.edu/Forecast/2023-04.pdf).

How El Niño forms. NOAA.

El Niño can also wreak havoc on the many marine ecosystems that support the
world’s fishing industries, including [coral
reefs](https://theconversation.com/watching-a-coral-reef-die-as-climate-
change-devastates-one-of-the-most-pristine-tropical-island-areas-on-
earth-159792) and [seagrass meadows](https://theconversation.com/restoring-
seagrasses-can-bring-coastal-bays-back-to-life-147798).

Specifically, El Niño tends to trigger intense and widespread periods of
extreme ocean warming known as marine heat waves.

Global ocean temperatures are already [near record
highs](https://climatereanalyzer.org/clim/sst_daily/), so El Niño-induced
marine heat waves could push many sensitive fisheries to a breaking point.

**What is a marine heat wave?**

A marine heat wave is just that: a “wave” of extreme heat in the ocean, not
dissimilar to an atmospheric heat wave on land.

At their smallest, marine heat waves can inundate [local bays and
coves](https://doi.org/10.1029/2019JC015673) with hotter-than-normal water for
a few days or weeks. At their largest, marine heat waves like the [Northeast
Pacific Warm Blob](https://doi.org/10.1002/2015GL063306) of 2013-2014 can grow
to gargantuan proportions, with regions [three times the size of
Texas](https://indd.adobe.com/view/ffe33cde-3628-42e8-adc2-eaf85d8312e4)
experiencing ocean temperatures 4 to 6 F (about 2 to 3 C) above average for
months or even years.

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/06/Screenshot-2026-06-21-at-10.50.38-AM-680x410.png)

Warm water might not seem like a big deal, especially to surfers hoping to
leave their wetsuits at home. But for many marine organisms that are highly
adapted to specific water temperatures, [marine heat waves can make living in
the ocean feel like running a marathon](https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-
marine-032122-121437).

For example, some fish increase their metabolism in warm waters by so much
that they burn energy faster than they can eat, and they can die. Pacific cod
declined by 70% in the Gulf of Alaska in response to a marine heat wave.
[Other impacts](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41558-019-0412-1) include bleached
corals, widespread harmful algal blooms, decimated seaweeds and increased
marine mammal strandings. All told, [billions of U.S. dollars are
lost](https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-marine-032122-121437) to marine heat
waves each year.

Marine heat waves flare up for a [variety of
reasons](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-019-10206-z). Sometimes, ocean
currents shift warm water around. Sometimes, surface winds are weaker than
normal, leading to less evaporation over the ocean and warmer waters.
Sometimes, cloudy places just aren’t as cloudy for a few months, which lets
more sunlight in and heats up the ocean. Sometimes, both weaker winds and
fewer clouds happen at the same time, producing [record-breaking marine heat
waves](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-020-15820-w).

**How does El Niño fit in?**

In the climate system, El Niño is king. When it dons its fiery crown, the
entire planet takes notice, and the oceans are no exception. But the
likelihood of increased marine heat wave activity during El Niño depends on
where you are.

Along the U.S. West Coast during El Niño, surface winds that normally blow
from the north tend to subside. This weakens evaporation and [slows
upwelling](https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/education/tutorial_currents/03coastal4.html)
of colder, deeper water. That increases the chances of coastal marine heat
waves. [California waters are already extremely
warm](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/may/22/marine-heatwave-west-
coast). El Niño could make things even hotter for longer.

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/06/Screenshot-2026-06-21-at-10.50.46-AM-680x564.png)

Peruvian fishers have for centuries weathered periods of extreme ocean warming
that drive fish away. [It wasn’t until the
1920s](https://earthobservatory.nasa.gov/features/ElNino/page3.php) that
scientists realized that these South American marine heat waves were related
to the Pacific-wide ENSO.

In the Bay of Bengal east of India, interactions between El Niño and a
tropical air flow pattern known as the [Walker
Circulation](https://www.climate.gov/news-features/blogs/enso/walker-
circulation-ensos-atmospheric-buddy) elevate the risk for marine heat waves.

**Seafloor heat waves are another risk**

Even if marine heat waves aren’t obvious at the ocean surface, that doesn’t
mean all is well down below.

In a [2023 study](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-023-36567-0), my colleagues
and I showed that marine heat waves also unfold along the seafloor of coastal
regions. In fact, these “bottom marine heat waves” are sometimes more intense
than their surface counterparts. They can also persist much longer. For
example, a 1997-1998 bottom marine heat wave off the U.S. West Coast lasted an
extra four to five months after surface ocean temperatures had already cooled.

Events like this can be related to El Niño and put a lot of stress on bottom-
dwelling species. Bering Sea snow crab landings were down 84% in 2018 after a
marine heat wave reached the seafloor.

**We’re in (for) hot water**

With El Niño on the horizon, what can we expect for this year?

The good news is [seasonal forecast models can skillfully predict marine heat
waves](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-022-04573-9) three to six months in
advance, depending on the region. And forecasts tend to be most accurate
during El Niño years.

[![Maps show increasing risk, particularly off California and in the Indian
Ocean. The Arctic Ocean also heats
up](https://images.theconversation.com/files/741441/original/file-20260611-57-sa1nql.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.0&q=45&auto=format&w=754&fit=clip)](https://images.theconversation.com/files/741441/original/file-20260611-57-sa1nql.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.0&q=45&auto=format&w=1000&fit=clip)Marine
heat wave forecasts from May 2026 show the probability, left, based on the
North American Multi-Model Ensemble, and magnitude, right, of marine heat
waves expected in 2026 and early 2027. Marine heat waves were already
developing off the Pacific Coasts of North, Central and South America as of
June 2026.  
[NOAA](https://psl.noaa.gov/marine-heatwaves/)

[The latest forecast](https://psl.noaa.gov/marine-heatwaves/) predicts several
marine heat waves developing as El Niño ramps up, with damaging heat reaching
close to half the global ocean by the end of 2026. The California and Mexican
coasts in particular have a very high likelihood of strong marine heat waves,
and the Indian Ocean and parts of the Southern Ocean are also likely to see
damaging heat.

These predictions are far enough out that conditions could change. Time will
tell whether they hold (hot) water, but we would do well to prepare.
